title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Roof soft washing
audience: Owners of small Australian roof soft washing businesses who need a base rate, a minimum charge and a flat-or-hourly decision before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from your own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Choose between a flat price and an hourly quote for a roof, and set a minimum charge for a short visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A roof soft washing rate depends on the storey and pitch, the access method, the chemicals and rinse work, the mould treatment you offer and the range of work you can book in one visit. A standard single-storey roof is a fixed-scope job, so a flat price can work. A steep, multi-storey or hard-to-access roof is harder to pin down, so an hourly quote can be fairer. Use the local evidence in the roof CP-01 and CP-04 lessons and the BP-05 lesson, not a national average. No roof-specific hourly band was found in this research, so do not borrow one from another trade.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every paid hour can be billed. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate paid hours for a year, then subtract non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (published 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours come from the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, the pump and hoses, access equipment and its upkeep, chemicals, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure. Have a registered tax agent confirm how they apply to your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to get the base rate. Review it each quarter and compare it with what clients accept.

instruction.heading: Flat price or hourly quote for a roof
instruction.body: Housecall Pro (vendor; country not stated) says flat rates suit repeat jobs with a clear scope, and recommends starting flat rates for the most common jobs. Airtasker's Australian handyman guide says hourly rates suit complex jobs and flat rates suit fixed-scope work. Apply both to roofs. A standard single-storey soft wash can be a flat price built from its hours, plus the chemical and rinse lines. A complex roof, one with an unusual pitch or a difficult access, is better quoted by the hour, with a stated estimate. Price the access before the flat price is set. Build the flat price from your hours, not from a published average.

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short jobs
instruction.body: A small roof, a single outbuilding or a visit that finds the roof is not ready still needs travel, set-up, access and checking. These do not shrink with the size of the job. Set a minimum that covers a short visit, and state it before the visit. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin. Its figures are labelled illustrative and are not used here. No roof-specific minimum was found. Airtasker's handyman minimum service fee of $80 to $120 is for handyman jobs, not roofs, and is not used here.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, pump and hoses, access equipment, chemicals, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income you need, with allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
For each roof, decide whether a flat price or an hourly quote fits its scope and access, and say which in the quote.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up, access and checking for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only. A single-storey roof is booked as a flat price, but on the site visit the roof has a steep pitch that needs a different access method and more time than the standard job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner keep the flat price, and what should the quote say?
workedExamples.reasoning: The flat price was built for a standard job, and the access now changes the hours. The owner switches this roof to an hourly quote for the access and the washing, with an estimate of hours and a stated basis, and says why. The owner does not absorb the difference, and does not start work until the access method is checked against the Victorian rule. A quote that changes after acceptance needs the client's written agreement.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the flat-price rules, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing every roof flat, including roofs whose access changes the hours.
commonErrors.prevention: Check access and pitch at the site visit, and switch to an hourly quote when the scope cannot be pinned down.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same price as a full roof, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up, access and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited. The ACCC guidance does not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and business costs with a registered tax agent.

Victoria: the Building and Plumbing Commission says a soft wash alone appears to be outside the roofing (stormwater) licence scope, and gutter or downpipe work appears inside roof drainage. That reading is not confirmed. Confirm the scope before you price any gutter or downpipe line. Victoria's working-at-height rules were not checked; check them with WorkSafe Victoria before you price a roof access.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
Each roof quote states whether it is flat or hourly, and a minimum charge is stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the flat-or-hourly rules, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Use a flat price for standard roofs, an hourly quote for complex access, and a stated minimum for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A roof soft washing owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short roof visit?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a roof soft washing base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Housecall Pro, 'Flat rate vs hourly', https://www.housecallpro.com/learn/flat-rate-vs-hourly/, published 2 February 2025, updated 7 October 2025. Vendor page; country not stated. Supports: flat rates suit repeat jobs with a clear scope.

Airtasker Australia, 'Handyman pricing guide', https://www.airtasker.com/au/guides/handyman-pricing/, last updated 13 March 2024. Supports: hourly for complex jobs, flat for fixed-scope work. Handyman guide; minimum fee not used for roofs.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Supports: minimum set from full visit cost and margin; figures labelled illustrative and not used.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Building and Plumbing Commission (Victoria), 'Roofing (stormwater) work', https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/plumbers/plumber-classes-and-categories/roofing-stormwater-work, last updated 30 June 2026. Supports: cleaning excluded from roofing work unless it connects, disconnects or alters the item.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law. Cited for the height point; the Victorian rule was not checked.

WorkSafe Victoria, news release on falls risks in the solar sector, https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2026-08/crackdown-falls-risks-solar-sector, 26 August 2026. Supports: allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Aimed at solar; the principle is stated for any roof.

Note: minimum and call-out charge rules for roofs, price display beyond the ACCC pricing page, and tax treatment of leave and superannuation are UNCONFIRMED. No roof-specific hourly band or minimum charge was found.
